Thank you so much for your feedback, we really appreciate the consideration! We are happy to see that we are aligned on the high potential impact of evaluating FMs on BPM applications, and that **WONDERBREAD** can help to address gaps in current benchmarks. We also also glad to see that you found our experimental setup and evaluations thorough.

We respond to each of the questions raised below:

### (1) The benchmark is based on narrow use cases (e.g., navigation in websites for e-commerce and content management) that are not necessarily representative of the wide variety of business processes in enterprises.

Please see our global response above on **(1) Dataset Diversity and Task Selection.**

We have also added the following paragraph to our **Discussion** section to suggest ways to build upon the blueprint laid out in **WONDERBREAD** and mitigate this issue in future versions of the dataset:

> To our knowledge, **WONDERBREAD** is currently the largest dataset for BPM tasks. However, it is still limited in its ability to capture the broad variety of real-world enterprise workflows. Scaling the approach outlined in this paper represents an exciting future research direction. We propose several ways to increase the size and diversity of data: (1) Synthetically generate demonstrations using AI agents trained on existing workflow examples and reject invalid demonstrations, as detailed in [8] [42]. (2) Crowdsource human demonstrations through platforms like Amazon Mechanical Turk. (3) Collaborate with a large enterprise willing to deploy our recording script to collect real-world workflows. (4) Scrape how-to videos and screen recordings of workflows from sites like Youtube.

### (2) It does not provide much detail about how the foundation models are actually used in the baseline experiments for the different tasks. For example, I would have liked to see a description of the prompts that were used for the different tasks (including for the LLM-based raters), what the challenges of prompt engineering were, whether the in-context-learning uses few shots, etc.

Please see our global response above on **(2) Details on Prompts Used for Experiments and Evaluations.**

In terms of challenges faced, we did have initial difficulty in getting our LLM-based automated evaluations to align with human ratings for several tasks, as noted in **Appendix Section C.2 - LLM-Based Evaluation: Question Answering**. We went through several rounds of prompt engineering in which we sampled a small subset of LLM-based evaluations, compared the ratings with human annotations, and identified common areas of disagreement. We then modified the prompt to emphasize certain desired behaviors (e.g. being harsher at grading on specific axes) and repeated this process twice before achieving the higher agreements demonstrated in **Appendix Table 8** and **Appendix Table 9**. Please also see the newly added **Appendix Section F** for full prompts used.

### (3) A limitation of the work is that it does not consider options such as parameter efficient tuning which can significantly improve quality

As all of the models used for our state-of-the-art baseline results were closed source, we did not have access to these models’ underlying weights and thus could not conduct any finetuning. However, this is definitely an interesting area for future research, and we are excited to see what methodological advances our benchmark and dataset inspired as well!

We appreciate your thorough feedback and insights! Your suggestions have significantly improved our manuscript, and we're grateful for the time you dedicated to reviewing our work. We are glad that to se that you appreciated the thoroughness of our evaluations and the depth of our coverage of BPM tasks. 

Below, we address each point you raised in your review:


### (1) Limited Data Diversity: The data is sourced from only four websites, which may not adequately represent the diversity of BPM scenarios and could limit the generalizability of the findings.

Please see our global response above on **(1) Dataset Diversity and Task Selection**.

First, **WONDERBREAD** is currently the largest BPM dataset assembled. So despite its limitations, we believe it still represents a valuable contribution to the field as-is.

Second, please note that despite collecting workflows from only 4 websites, we curate a diverse set of 6 BPM scenarios covering workflow documentation, knowledge transfer, and improvement. These BPM tasks are formulated in a general, workflow agnostic manner (i.e. "documenting a workflow" is a skill that can be applied to any workflow regardless of its source website or application). Thus, as more workflows are added to **WONDERBREAD** these tasks can be seamlessly reapplied to them.

Third, we believe that the 4 websites we use provide fairly decent coverage of typical digital tasks. These websites are sourced from the WebArena [2] benchmark, a popular workflow automation benchmark that contains self-hosted clones of Adobe Magento (an enterprise content management system), Gitlab (an enterprise code repository), Postmill (a forum), and an ecommerce website. While these sites do not cover the entire space of enterprise workflows, they contain non-trivial workflows representative of general digital tasks (the SOTA model has a success rate of 35% [1])

There are several advantages from using these 4 web applications as the source of our dataset. First, these websites are free and can be self-hosted, which enables fairer benchmarking and reproducibility (in contrast to enterprise workflows which require proprietary or pay-to-use software). Second, these websites are shared with another well-known benchmark called WebArena [2] which has been well-studied in the automation literature, and thus our dataset can also be utilized by researchers building automation agents.

[1] Sodhi, Paloma, et al. ‘SteP: Stacked LLM Policies for Web Actions’.​​[2] Zhou, Shuyan, et al. "Webarena: A realistic web environment for building autonomous agents."


### (2) Insufficient Scalability Analysis: The paper does not discuss how model performance might scale with an increased number of training examples.

The primary focus of this first version of **WONDERBREAD** was benchmarking and evaluation, and thus we do not do any model training in our experiments. This meant that measuring the impact of scaling our dataset on model training fell outside the scope of this initial work.

However, we do agree that the ~3,000 high quality workflow demonstrations in **WONDERBREAD** would be extremely useful in training future BPM and workflow automation models. As the focus of this paper was on datasets + benchmarks, however, we left answering such methodological questions to future work. We are equally excited to see how the performance of models built on our dataset scale!

### (3) Considering the current limitations in data diversity and volume, what strategies are proposed or could be considered to scale the size of the dataset to enhance model training and performance?

This is a great question -- There are several strategies that could be used to scale the size of the **WONDERBREAD** dataset for improved model training and performance. We have added the following paragraph to our Discussion section in response:

> To our knowledge, **WONDERBREAD** is currently the largest dataset for BPM tasks. However, it is still limited in its ability to capture the broad variety of real-world enterprise workflows. Scaling the approach outlined in this paper represents an exciting future research direction. We propose several ways to increase the size and diversity of data: (1) Synthetically generate demonstrations using AI agents trained on existing workflow examples and reject invalid demonstrations, as detailed in [8] [42]. (2) Crowdsource human demonstrations through platforms like Amazon Mechanical Turk. (3) Collaborate with a large enterprise willing to deploy our recording script to collect real-world workflows. (4) Scrape how-to videos and screen recordings of workflows from sites like Youtube.

[8] Bai, Hao, et al. "Digirl: Training in-the-wild device-control agents with autonomous reinforcement learning." arXiv preprint arXiv:2406.11896 (2024).

[42] Pan, Jiayi, et al. "Autonomous evaluation and refinement of digital agents." arXiv preprint arXiv:2404.06474 (2024).

We agree that adding more diverse data is an important direction for future research, and will aim to increase the depth and breadth of data in future versions of **WONDERBREAD**. Given its status as the “first” benchmark for BPM tasks (4WGS25), we believe **WONDERBREAD** is still a useful step forward for the field despite not covering every possible enterprise workflow. 

Going forward, **WONDERBREAD** offers a blueprint for compiling an even more diverse dataset. In response to these questions, we have added the following paragraph to our **Discussion** section outlining ways to increase the diversity of data in future versions of **WONDERBREAD**:

> To our knowledge, **WONDERBREAD** is currently the largest dataset for BPM tasks. However, it is still limited in its ability to capture the broad variety of real-world enterprise workflows. Scaling the approach outlined in this paper represents an exciting future research direction. We propose several ways to increase the size and diversity of data: (1) Synthetically generate demonstrations using AI agents trained on existing workflow examples and reject invalid demonstrations, as detailed in [8] [42]. (2) Crowdsource human demonstrations through platforms like Amazon Mechanical Turk. (3) Collaborate with a large enterprise willing to deploy our recording script to collect real-world workflows. (4) Scrape how-to videos and screen recordings of workflows from sites like Youtube.

Additionally, an important distinction to note is that although the workflows being demonstrated in **WONDERBREAD** do not capture every possible enterprise workflow, the 6 BPM tasks which we define on top of these workflows are very diverse and do cover a wide range of enterprise use cases. As detailed in **Section 4 - Benchmarks**, these tasks are defined as follows:

1. Automatically generating documentation for a workflow (“SOP Generation”)
2. Segmenting a video demonstration into discrete workflows (“Demo Segmentation”)
3. Answering arbitrary questions about a workflow (“Question Answering”)
4. Validating that a workflow was successfully completed (“Demo Validation”)
5. Ranking workflow executions sourced from across different annotators (“SOP Ranking”)
6. Improving standard operating procedures (“SOP Improvement”). 

This is a fairly general set of capabilities, and by far the largest set of BPM tasks assembled into a single benchmark. As noted by reviewer (nBnV21), our benchmark covers the “entire lifecycle” of BPM projects and thus offers significantly greater dataset and task diversity than prior work focused solely on end-to-end automation (as shown in **Table 1**).

Another question the reviewers had is why our workflows are sourced from 4 websites. These websites are sourced from the WebArena [2] benchmark, and are self-hosted clones of Adobe Magento (an enterprise content management system), Gitlab (an enterprise code repository), Postmill (a forum), and an ecommerce website. Second, these websites are shared with another well-known benchmark called WebArena [2] which has been well-studied in the automation literature, and thus our dataset can also be utilized by researchers building automation agents. 

[1] Sodhi, Paloma, et al. ‘SteP: Stacked LLM Policies for Web Actions’.
​​[2] Zhou, Shuyan, et al. "Webarena: A realistic web environment for building autonomous agents."

There were several questions asking for more details on our experimental setup, e.g. the specific prompts used for generating model outputs, the prompts used for our LLM-based evaluations, etc. We thank our reviewers for pointing out these areas of confusion, and we have added significant detail to our manuscript to make this clearer to the reader in response -- our paper is much stronger thanks to these suggestions. In particular, we have added all prompts used to **Appendix Section F** in response. 

This **Appendix Section F** now includes all prompts utilized in our benchmark, organized by task, for both generating model outputs and evaluating them. For each prompt utilized, we also include a brief description and a link to where the prompt exists in our codebase within our public Github repository for quick reference.

> Our initial results show that current multimodal FMs, including GPT-4, Gemini, and Claude, excel at generating documentation which captures the higher-level characteristics of workflows but struggle with finer-grained analyses such as question answering and workflow quality assessment. ### (10) In the "Demo Segmentation", "Question Answering", and "Demo Ranking" tasks, two situations (multiple demos and single demo) are both involved in these tasks. Is it necessary to distinguish between the two to calculate performance?

Apologies for the confusion -- for the **“Demo Segmentation”** and **“Demo Ranking”** (aka **“SOP Ranking”**) tasks, our experiments only consider multiple demos. ### (11) What is the meaning of "V-Measure" in Figure 4? Why does the additional information to the model in the form of an SOP and intent decrease performance for Gemini Pro 1? Is additional information necessary?

V-Measure is the harmonic mean of homogeneity (how similar the contents of a cluster are to each other) and completeness (how well samples of the same class are grouped into the same cluster). It ranges from 0 (low quality clustering) to 1 (high quality clustering), and is formally defined as follows: $V = 2 * \frac{h * c}{h + c}$ with $h = 1 - \frac{H(C | K)}{H(C)}$ and $c = 1 - \frac{H(K | C)}{H(K)}$ where $H(x)$ is the entropy of $x$ and $C$ are the classes while $K$ are the clusters.

This additional information is not necessary for segmenting the demonstrations. We hypothesize that the additional information causes a decrease in performance for GeminiPro by distracting it from the count of states that it needs to assign to tasks. This is supported by the following analysis of the number of blanks in GeminiPro’s response (i.e. the number of states that it does not assign to any workflow), which indicates that this number increases the more information is provided in the prompt for GeminiPro:

| Input Format | Count of Blanks for Demo Segmentation task |
|------------|--------------|
| TD+KF+SOP  |    298 |
KF+SOP  |   100 |
KF   |  30 |

We consider any state that does not have an explicit assignment to be incorrect. Thus, the model is penalized for abstaining from state assignments. In fact, we find four demonstrations in which GeminiPro gave a completely blank response: 539 @ 2024-01-07-17-04-44, 350 @ 2024-01-04-18-16-40, 468 @ 2024-01-06-15-26-01, 333 @ 2024-01-01-13-19-13

We have added a note to this effect in the results of **Section 5.2 - Knowledge Transfer:**

> On inspection, we find that the frequency at which Gemini Pro outputs blank state mappings (i.e. to not assign a keyframe to any candidate workflow, which under our evaluation framework gets penalized as an incorrect mapping) increases with longer prompts, thus indicating a worse ability to follow the full context of the prompt.

### (7) In the SOP Generation Description task, you said there are two kinds of input, (w,(s1,...,sn)) or (w,(s1,a1,...an-1,sn)), but only one performance table for SOP Generation (Table 3) is provided. What is the performance for the other situation?

Apologies for the confusion -- to clarify, we have renamed $w$ to $I$ (for “intent”) and thus there are three types of inputs that we evaluate: (1) intent only -- $(I)$, (2) intent plus screenshots -- $(I, (s_1, ..., s_n))$, (3) intent plus screenshots plus actions -- $(I, (s_1, a_1, ..., a_{n-1}, s_n))$.

We have added the following sentence to **Appendix Section B.1 -- SOP Generation Description** to clarify the mapping between these input formats and our results:

> Given a demonstration $d = (I, SOP,  (s_1, a_1, s_2, a_2, ..., a_{n-1}, s_n))$, we provide the model with either $(I)$, $(I, (s_1, ..., s_n))$, or $(I, (s_1, a_1, ..., a_{n-1}, s_n))$. In our Results Table 3, these correspond to rows with one checkmark under the "Intent" column, two checkmarks under the "Intent" and "Keyframes" columns, and three checkmarks under the "Intent", "Keyframes", and "Trace" columns, respectively.

### (8) The prompt of LLM for making the output answers for each task is missing. Could you please add the prompts and explain how to get and parse the answer in each task?

In response to this feedback, we have included all prompts in the **Appendix Section F** of our manuscript.  The prompt for each task explicitly describes the form of the response that is expected from the model, which is generally either a JSON type dictionary with a specific structure or a stand alone output (such as a number or letter). We have included brief descriptions with each prompt that indicate which output is expected in this new section.

### (9) Why are open source LLMs not involved in the evaluation? Whether only three LLMs are limited?

For our initial baseline results, we focused on the three most capable state-of-the-art models to provide the strongest possible baselines -- namely, Claude, GPT-4, and Gemini. These all happened to be closed source models, but they are publicly accessible via APIs (which we leverage for our paper). 

We believe that this approach was merited for establishing a strong baseline to which future models (both open and closed source) can be compared. Additionally, as a multimodal benchmark, our tasks heavily depend on a model being able to process interleaved text and images. To our knowledge, there aren’t capable open source VLMs that accept interleaved text and images as input. Please also see **Table 3** in [1] (another benchmark that did not use open source models for interleaved text/images). 

However, we do agree that developing new open source models with these capabilities is an important area of future research, and we look forward to adding them to our benchmark as they are developed. 

And if there is a specific model you would like to see evaluated, please let us know and we will be happy to include it in our baseline results!

[1] Lin, Kevin Qinghong, et al. "VideoGUI: A Benchmark for GUI Automation from Instructional Videos." arXiv preprint arXiv:2406.10227 (2024).

### (4) What is the basis for setting these 6 novel tasks? Is there any reference?

Thank you so much for the incredibly detailed comments and feedback. Going through all of your suggestions has greatly strengthened our manuscript, and we sincerely thank you for your time and attention to detail when reviewing our paper. We have added a significant number of new figures and additional content thanks to your suggestions. We are glad to see that you resonated with the effort put into ensuring the high quality of our dataset, as well as your appreciation for our automated LLM-based evaluation framework. We respond to each of the issues raised in your review below:

### (1) Could you use an example, such as a physician submitting a medication order, to explain in detail what the four stages of BPM do, so as to accelerate the understanding of BPM?

Thank you for the suggestion. We have added the following to **Appendix Section A.6 -- Example Hypothetical BPM Project** to provide a concrete example of what each stage of BPM might entail for a hypothetical project:

> For clarity, we provide the following as an example of what a hypothetical BPM project might entail. Let’s say a hospital wants to accelerate the workflow by which admitted patients have their insurance verified. Today, the process is done completely manually by a team of billing specialists. The workflow involves copying the patient’s demographic information into several databases and visiting an insurer’s web portal to verify that the patient’s insurance coverage is accurate and up-to-date. A hypothetical BPM project for accelerating this workflow might progress as follows: (1) Documentation: First, a business development (BD) analyst interviews all of the billing specialists on the team, conducts shadowing sessions over Zoom, and watches screen recordings collected by the team in order to create written documentation of the insurance verification workflow. (2) Knowledge Transfer: After creating a draft of the workflow, the BD analyst hosts a series of in-person brainstorming sessions with the team; the BD analyst identifies several gaps in her current understanding of the workflow, and they collaboratively arrive at a shared consensus of all steps involved in the end-to-end workflow. (3) Improvement: From these conversations, the BD analyst identifies several bottlenecks and inefficiencies; for example, entering the patient’s demographic information into multiple databases that could instead be automatically synced, or waiting for the approval of another department that has a turnaround of one week but isn’t strictly necessary. The BD analyst then draws a new, more streamlined workflow diagram and shares her findings with the billing team to implement. (4) Automation: Based on these observations, the billing team believes that several of the subtasks within this new workflow might be automatable. They enlist the help of the hospital’s IT department to build an integration between their two database applications to automate this data entry. They also work on developing a robotic process automation (RPA) bot that can navigate multiple screens to automatically submit forms to insurers.

### (2) Could you show some examples of qualitative analysis, such as success and failure cases?

This is a great suggestion, thank you for the comment! In response, we have added **Appendix Figure 11** and **Appendix Figure 12**, which provide examples of success and failure cases for two of our tasks, as well as line-by-line qualitative analysis of GPT-4 and Claude model outputs.

### (3) In Workflow Selection, why tasks that include multiple websites from WebArena are ignored? Could you please explain in detail how the excluded workflows are designed to be impossible, underspecified, or have incorrect evaluations.

Thank you for the comment, we should have clarified this better. In response, we have added the following paragraph to **Appendix A.2.1 Workflow Selection**:

> First, several workflows in WebArena are designed to be impossible. These are the workflows that have a correct answer marked as "N/A". For example, one workflow has the intent "What are the main criticisms of this product?'' and marks the correct answer as "N/A" since there are no criticisms. We remove all of these workflows. An example of a \textit{de facto} impossible workflow is "Assign the issue regarding flash alerts to myself and primer.'' Though there is a non-N/A answer for this workflow, upon manual inspection we found that the Gitlab interface does not actually allow issues to be assigned to more than one user, and thus we removed it from our dataset. Underspecified workflows are those whose answer we found arbitrary upon manual inspection. For example, an intent such as "Show me the email address of the customer who is the most unhappy with Circe fleece'' is underspecified as the phrase "most unhappy'' is unquantifiable when there are multiple one-star reviews. We remove all of these underspecified workflows. Finally, we exclude workflows that have valid intents but whose expected answers were deemed incorrect upon manual inspection. Example workflows from the Webarena dataset with these mistakes include "the number of commits of the contributor who has the most commits to branch main'' in Gitlab being stated incorrectly or that "the amount spent on home decoration shopping during 1/29/2023'' being calculated incorrectly are also excluded. Finally, we ignore the 23 workflows in  WebArena that include multiple websites. We do this for simplicity as our recording script could only handle one website at a time. This left us with a final total of 598 workflows.

summary_and_contributions.value: This paper introduces WONDERBREAD, pioneering the first comprehensive benchmark designed to assess multimodal models across a spectrum of typical process mining tasks. This benchmark encompasses a rich dataset of 2,928 human demonstrations that span videos, images, and textual data, complemented by detailed step-by-step guides known as Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) and exhaustive action logs. Their emphasis is on the practical application of these models to three pivotal Business Process Management (BPM) tasks—documentation, knowledge transfer, and process enhancement—which have been notably understated in current Machine Learning (ML) benchmarks for workflow automation. WONDERBREAD features an automated evaluation harness with programmatic metrics and LLM-based assessments, providing baseline results for state-of-the-art multimodal models.

summary_and_contributions.value: The paper presents WONDERBREAD, the first benchmark designed specifically for evaluating multimodal LLMs in business process management (BPM) tasks beyond mere automation. Existing ML benchmarks in BPM predominantly focus on full end-to-end automation, while this benchmark addresses more varied BPM functions such as documentation and process improvement. The benchmark includes a dataset of 2928 human-annotated workflow demonstrations and introduces six novel BPM tasks derived from real-world applications. The evaluation results reveal that while state-of-the-art FMs excel at generating documentation, they underperform in tasks requiring the validation of workflow completion.

review.value: WONDERBREAD introduces a pioneering benchmark for evaluating multimodal foundation models on diverse BPM tasks, effectively addressing critical gaps in the field, though it falls short on data diversity and scalability analysis.

strengths.value:
- The introduction is clearly written and effectively identifies the significant gap in BPM research and practice, which well motivates this work.
- This paper introduces the first benchmark for evaluating multimodal LLMs on diverse BPM tasks, using a human-annotated dataset that includes intent, recording, action trace, key frames, and standard operating procedures (SOPs).
- Six novel BPM tasks are defined, covering a range from workflow documentation to knowledge transfer and process improvement, with a thorough evaluation of these tasks against state-of-the-art LLMs.

- Limited Data Diversity: The data is sourced from only four websites, which may not adequately represent the diversity of BPM scenarios and could limit the generalizability of the findings.
- Insufficient Scalability Analysis: The paper does not discuss how model performance might scale with an increased number of training examples.

summary_and_contributions.value: This paper provides a comprehensive benchmark for measuring the effectiveness of foundation models to document, improve and automate business processes. review.value:
This paper provides a comprehensive benchmark for measuring the effectiveness of foundation models to document, improve and automate business processes. This is potentially very impactful since foundation models are revolutionizing the way that businesses work, yet there is still little work to measure how they impact business processes. 

The paper is very well written and the description of the benchmark is easy to follow. Some of the strengths of the paper include:

- While other benchmarks focus only on workflow automation, this paper focuses on the entire lifecycle of a business process including documentation, knowledge transfer, improvement and automation. The paper offers a detailed comparison with previous benchmarks (Table 1)

- The dataset and experiments are published and made available in github. The dataset has a large number of demonstrations (2928) by human experts. 

- The experimental evaluation is very thorough, with lots of supporting material in the Appendix 

- Baseline results are provided using state-of-the-art foundation models 

On the other hand, some of the weaknesses of the paper include:

- The benchmark is based on narrow use cases (e.g., navigation in websites for e-commerce and content management) that are not necessarily representative of the wide variety of business processes in enterprises.

- It does not provide much detail about how the foundation models are actually used in the baseline experiments for the different tasks. For example, I would have liked to see a description of the prompts that were used for the different tasks (including for the LLM-based raters), what the challenges of prompt engineering were, whether the in-context-learning uses few shots, etc. 

- A limitation of the work is that it does not consider options such as parameter efficient tuning which can significantly improve quality

title.value: WONDERBREAD: A Benchmark for Evaluating Multimodal Foundation Models on Business Process Management Tasks

TLDR.value: A benchmark + dataset for evaluating multimodal models on process mining tasks such as workflow documentation, knowledge transfer, and process improvement, with ~3k human workflow demonstrations + manually written SOPs + automated evaluations.

abstract.value: Existing ML benchmarks lack the depth and diversity of annotations needed for evaluating models on business process management (BPM) tasks. BPM is the practice of documenting, measuring, improving, and automating enterprise workflows. However, research has focused almost exclusively on one task -- full end-to-end automation using agents based on multimodal foundation models (FMs) like GPT-4. This focus on automation ignores the reality of how most BPM tools are applied today -- simply documenting the relevant workflow takes 60% of the time of the typical process optimization project. To address this gap we present WONDERBREAD, the first benchmark for evaluating multimodal FMs on BPM tasks beyond automation. Our contributions are: (1) a dataset containing 2928 documented workflow demonstrations; (2) 6 novel BPM tasks sourced from real-world applications ranging from workflow documentation to knowledge transfer to process improvement; and (3) an automated evaluation harness. Our benchmark shows that while state-of-the-art FMs can automatically generate documentation (e.g. recalling 88% of the steps taken in a video demonstration of a workflow), they struggle to re-apply that knowledge towards finer-grained validation of workflow completion (F1 < 0.3). We hope WONDERBREAD encourages the development of more "human-centered" AI tooling for enterprise applications and furthers the exploration of multimodal FMs for the broader universe of BPM tasks. We publish our dataset and experiments here: https://github.com/HazyResearch/wonderbread

def process(client, invitation):

    domain = client.get_group(invitation.domain)
    venue_id = domain.id
    submission_venue_id = domain.content['submission_venue_id']['value']
    venue_name = domain.content['title']['value']

    now = openreview.tools.datetime_millis(datetime.datetime.utcnow())
    cdate = invitation.cdate

    if cdate > now:
        ## invitation is in the future, do not process
        print('invitation is not yet active', cdate)
        return

    def post_submission_edit(submission):

        updated_note = openreview.api.Note(
            id=submission.id
        )

        if invitation.edit['note']['readers'] == ['everyone'] and submission.odate is None:
            updated_note.odate = now
            updated_note.content = {
                '_bibtex': {
                    'value': openreview.tools.generate_bibtex(
                        note=submission,
                        venue_fullname=venue_name,
                        year=str(datetime.datetime.utcnow().year),
                        url_forum=submission.forum,
                        paper_status='under review',
                        anonymous='readers' in submission.content['authors'] or 'readers' in invitation.edit.get('note', {}).get('content', {}).get('authors', {})
                    )
                }
            }

        client.post_note_edit(
            invitation=invitation.id,
            note=updated_note,
            signatures=[venue_id]
        )
    
    ## Release the submissions to specified readers if venueid is still submission
    submissions = client.get_all_notes(content= { 'venueid': submission_venue_id })
    print(f'update {len(submissions)} submissions')
    openreview.tools.concurrent_requests(post_submission_edit, submissions, desc='post_submission_edit')
